questions.prompt: What is the impulse response \(h(t)\) of an LTI system?
options: The output of the system when the input is a delta function \(\delta(t)\)
The output when the input is a unit step \(u(t)\)
The output when the input is a sinusoid at \(1\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\)
The derivative of the input signal
questions.explanation:
\(h(t)\) ≡ \(L[\delta(t)]\): you 'hit' the system with an ideal very short, very tall impulse (like a hammer blow) and record the response. For an LTI system, \(h(t)\) contains all the information about the system.
• The response to a step is the STEP response (related to h by integration).
• A sinusoid probes the frequency response, not the impulse response.

questions.prompt: An LTI system has impulse response \(h(t)\) and is driven by \(x(t)\). The output \(y(t)\) is given by…
options: the product \(y(t)=h(t)\cdot x(t)\)
the sum \(y(t)=h(t)+x(t)\)
the ratio \(y(t)=x(t)/h(t)\)
the convolution \(y(t)=\int h(t-\tau)x(\tau)\ d\tau\)  (written \(h\ast x\))
questions.explanation:
Write x as a sum of weighted, shifted impulses, then use linearity and time invariance: \(y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\ d\tau=(h\ast x)(t)\).
A pointwise product, sum, or ratio of the two functions would not respect the system's memory.

questions.prompt: A pure delay system has impulse response \(h(t)=\delta(t-2\ \mathrm{ms})\), so \(y(t)=x(t-2\ \mathrm{ms})\). It is driven by \(x(t)=\cos(2\pi\cdot 250\cdot t)\). What is the output at \(t=2.5\ \mathrm{ms}\)?
questions.explanation:
Convolving with a shifted delta delays the input: \(y(t)=x(t-2\ \mathrm{ms})\). At \(t=2.5\ \mathrm{ms}\), \(y=x(0.5\ \mathrm{ms})=\cos(2\pi\times 250\times 0.0005)=\cos(\pi/4)=0.7071\).
Common mistake: evaluating x at \(2.5\ \mathrm{ms}\ (\cos(5\pi/4)=-0.707)\), i.e., forgetting to delay.

questions.prompt: A sampled LTI system (samples every 1 ms) has impulse response \(h[0]=2\), \(h[1]=1\) (and \(h=0\) afterward). The input samples are \(x[0]=1\), \(x[1]=2\), \(x[2]=3\). Using \(y[n]=\Sigma\ x[k]\cdot h[n-k]\), what is y[2] (the output at \(t=2\ \mathrm{ms}\))?
questions.explanation:
\(y[2]=x[0]h[2]+x[1]h[1]+x[2]h[0]=(1)(0)+(2)(1)+(3)(2)=0+2+6=8\).
Each input sample launches a delayed copy of h, and y[2] adds all contributions that are present at time index 2. A common error is to pair the samples without reversing the index \((x[0]h[0]+x[1]h[1]+x[2]h[2]=2+2+0=4)\).

questions.prompt: An LTI system has impulse response \(h(t)=3e^{-t/2\ \mathrm{ms}}\cdot u(t)\) (per unit-weight impulse). The input is two impulses: \(x(t)=2\delta(t)+1\delta(t-1\ \mathrm{ms})\). What is the output at \(t=3\ \mathrm{ms}\)?
questions.explanation:
By linearity and time invariance, \(y(t)=2h(t)+1\cdot h(t-1\ \mathrm{ms})\).
At \(t=3\ \mathrm{ms}\): \(2h(3\ \mathrm{ms})=2\cdot 3e^{-1.5}=1.339\); \(h(2\ \mathrm{ms})=3e^{-1}=1.104\).
Sum \(=2.442\).
Common mistake: using h(3 ms) for both impulses, forgetting that the second impulse started only 2 ms ago.
questions.figure_alt: Decaying exponential impulse response starting at 3 with a 2 millisecond time constant.

questions.prompt: Which of these impulse responses could belong to a CAUSAL LTI system?
options: \(h(t)=e^{-t}\cdot u(t)\)
\(h(t)=\delta(t+2\ \mathrm{ms})\)
questions.explanation:
A causal system cannot respond before the input arrives. The impulse is applied at \(t=0\), so \(h(t)\) must be 0 for all t < 0. \(e^{-t}u(t)\) satisfies this.
• \(e^{-|t|}\) is nonzero for t < 0 (it would be a response before the impulse).
• u(t + 1) turns on at \(t=-1\), so the response begins before \(t=0\).
• \(\delta(t+2\ \mathrm{ms})\) is a response 2 ms BEFORE the impulse: it would need to see the future.

questions.prompt: A unit-height rectangular pulse lasting from \(t=0\) to 2 ms is applied to an LTI system whose impulse response is a rectangle \(h(t)=500\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\) for 0 < t < 2 ms (zero elsewhere), so \(\int h\ dt=1\). What does the output look like?
options: A rectangle from 0 to 2 ms with height 1
A triangle from 0 to 4 ms, peaking at 1 at \(t=2\ \mathrm{ms}\)
A triangle from 0 to 2 ms, peaking at 0.5
A rectangle from 0 to 4 ms with height 1
questions.explanation:
Convolving two equal-width rectangles gives a triangle whose total duration is the SUM of the widths: \(2\ \mathrm{ms}+2\ \mathrm{ms}=4\ \mathrm{ms}\).
Here h is a 'moving-average' filter (area 1): the output at time t is the average of the input over the previous 2 ms. It rises linearly while the window slides into the pulse, reaches 1 when the window is exactly over the pulse \((t=2\ \mathrm{ms})\), then falls linearly to 0 at \(t=4\ \mathrm{ms}\).
• A rectangle from 0 to 2 ms would be the output of a memoryless system.
• A 2 ms-wide triangle ignores that durations add.
• A 4 ms rectangle ignores that the window only fully overlaps the pulse at one instant.

questions.prompt: An LTI system has impulse response \(h(t)=(1/\tau)e^{-t/\tau}u(t)\). To compute the output \(y(t_{0})\) at some time \(t_{0}\) from the input, which input value is given the LARGEST weight?
options: The present value \(x(t_{0})\); older values are weighted by an exponentially decaying factor
The value at \(t=0\), because that is when the impulse was applied
A future value \(x(t_{0}+\tau)\), because the system anticipates the input
All past values equally, so the system just averages them
questions.explanation:
\(y(t_{0})=\int x(\tau')h(t_{0}-\tau')\ d\tau'\). The weight on the input value from T seconds ago is \(h(T)=(1/\tau)e^{-T/\tau}\). It is largest at \(T=0\) (the present) and fades with time constant \(\tau\): the system 'remembers' about the last \(\tau\) seconds.
• The system is causal, so no future values contribute (\(h=0\) for negative T).
• The weighting is not uniform; old values are gradually forgotten.
• There is no special significance of \(t=0\) for a time-invariant system.
questions.figure_alt: Exponentially decaying weight versus how long ago an input value occurred.

questions.prompt: An LTI system has impulse response \(h(t)=100\cdot e^{-t/5\ \mathrm{ms}}\cdot u(t)\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\). A constant input \(x=2\) has been applied for a very long time. What is the steady output?
questions.explanation:
For a constant input, \(y=x\cdot\int h(\tau)d\tau\): the DC gain of an LTI system is the AREA under its impulse response.
\(\int_{0}^{\infty}100e^{-\tau/5\ \mathrm{ms}}\ d\tau=100\times 5\ \mathrm{ms}=0.5\) (dimensionless). So \(y=2\times 0.5=1\).
Common mistake: using \(h(0)=100\) as the gain, or forgetting the time-constant factor when integrating.

questions.prompt: Preview of step response. A 'moving-average' system has impulse response \(h(t)=250\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\) for 0 < t < 4 ms (zero elsewhere). A step of height 3 is applied at \(t=0\). Using the convolution integral \(y(t)=\int x(t-\tau)h(\tau)d\tau\), find the output at \(t=3\ \mathrm{ms}\). (A later skill shows that the step response is the running integral of h.)
questions.explanation:
For t > 0 and a step input, \(x(t-\tau)=3\) for \(\tau<t\) and 0 for \(\tau>t\). So \(y(t)=\) 3·∫₀^min(t, \(4\ \mathrm{ms})\ h(\tau)d\tau\).
At \(t=3\ \mathrm{ms}\) (still inside the window): \(y=3\times 250\times 0.003=2.25\). After \(t=4\ \mathrm{ms}\) the output stops growing and stays at \(3\times 250\times 0.004=3\).
Common mistake: using the full window (3) at 3 ms, as if all of h had already contributed.

questions.prompt: Preview of the frequency-domain view. Drive a pure delay system \(h(t)=\delta(t-T)\), \(T=0.5\ \mathrm{ms}\), with the complex exponential \(e^{j\omega t}\). Convolution gives \(y=e^{j\omega(t-T)}=e^{-j\omega T}\cdot e^{j\omega t}\), so \(H(j\omega)=e^{-j\omega T}\). What is the phase \(\angle H\) in degrees at \(f=250\ \mathrm{Hz}\)?
questions.explanation:
\(\angle H=-\omega T=-2\pi(250)(0.0005)=-0.7854\ \mathrm{rad}=-45^{\circ}\).
A pure delay therefore gives a phase shift that grows linearly with frequency, with magnitude \(|H|=1\) (it passes every tone unchanged in size). Common mistake: using f instead of \(\omega\ (-0.125\ \mathrm{rad})\).

questions.prompt: Preview of transfer functions. Two pure-delay systems (delays 1 ms and 2.5 ms) are cascaded. The overall impulse response is the convolution of the two individual ones, \(\delta(t-1\ \mathrm{ms})\ast\delta(t-2.5\ \mathrm{ms})\). If the input is \(x(t)=\cos(2\pi\cdot 100\cdot t)\ \mathrm{V}\), what is the output at \(t=4\ \mathrm{ms}\)?
questions.explanation:
Convolving two shifted deltas adds the shifts: \(\delta(t-T_{1})\ast\delta(t-T_{2})=\delta(t-(T_{1}+T_{2}))\). The total delay is 3.5 ms.
\(y(4\ \mathrm{ms})=x(4\ \mathrm{ms}-3.5\ \mathrm{ms})=x(0.5\ \mathrm{ms})=\cos(2\pi\cdot 100\cdot 0.0005)=\cos(0.3142)=\cos 18^{\circ}=0.9511\ \mathrm{V}\).
In the frequency domain this is \(H_{1}H_{2}=e^{-j\omega T_{1}}e^{-j\omega T_{2}}\): convolution in time ↔ multiplication in frequency.
